questions.question: Identify the synonym of 'Brisk':
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Energetic**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"brisk"** means quick and active, full of energy, or marked by speed and efficiency. (तेज, फुर्तीला)
 
 
• **Example:** She took a brisk walk in the morning to stay healthy.
 
 
• **"Energetic"** refers to someone or something that is full of energy, enthusiasm, or vitality. (ऊर्जावान)
 
 
• **Example:** The children were energetic and excited during the outdoor games.
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the synonym of **'brisk'** is **'energetic'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Energetic**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Lazy** (आलसी): Someone who is unwilling to work or use energy.
 
 
• **Example:** He is too lazy to clean his room regularly.
 
 
 
 
• **Dull** (नीरस): Something lacking brightness, vividness, or excitement.
 
 
• **Example:** The lecture was so dull that many students fell asleep.
 
 
 
 
• **Slow** (धीमा): Moving or operating at a low speed or pace.
 
 
• **Example:** The internet connection was too slow to load the website.
 
 

2f:Td85,

सही उत्तर है: **ऊर्जावान (Energetic)**।

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with suitable preposition:
We are going ___ a vacation next week.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The correct preposition to use with "vacation" in this context is **"on"**, as it indicates that someone is going away for a holiday or break.
 
• Using "at," "in," or "for" would not fit here, as they do not convey the intended meaning of going for a vacation or trip.
 
• The phrase "going on a vacation" is a standard and grammatically correct expression in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"We are going **on** a vacation next week."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Preposition Usage:**
 
 
• **At:** Used to refer to a specific location (e.g., "at the park").
 
• **In:** Used to indicate being inside a space or area (e.g., "in the building").
 
• **For:** Used to indicate purpose or intent (e.g., "for a meeting").
 
 
 
• Only **on** is appropriate in the context of this sentence, as it is used to refer to planned trips or vacations.
</ul

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with most appropriate tense:
If you study hard, you ___ the exam.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence provided is an example of the **first conditional**, which is used to describe real or possible situations in the future.
 
• In the first conditional sentence structure, the **if-clause** uses the present simple tense, and the result clause uses **"will + base verb."**
 
• The correct structure for this sentence is: **If + Present Simple, will + base verb**.
 
• Among the options provided, **"will pass"** fits the required structure and conveys the correct meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *If you study hard, you **will pass** the exam.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **1st Conditional Sentence:**
 
 
• **Structure:** If + Present Simple, will + base verb.
 
• **Example:** If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
 
• **Usage:** Describes real or possible situations in the future with likely outcomes.
 
 
 
• **2nd Conditional Sentence:**
 
 
• **Structure:** If + Past Simple, would + base verb.
 
• **Example:** If I were rich, I would travel the world.
 
• **Usage:** Refers to hypothetical or imaginary situations in the present or future.
 
 
 
• **3rd Conditional Sentence:**
 
 
• **Structure:** If + Past Perfect, would have + past participle.
 
• **Example:** If she had studied harder, she would have passed the exam.
 
• **Usage:** Refers to unreal past situations and their imagined outcomes.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: The word "**bark**" can refer to a dog's sound or the outer layer of a tree. This is an example of ___.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word "**bark**" is an example of a **homonym**.
 
• A **homonym** is a word that is spelled and pronounced the same as another word but has a different meaning and often a different origin.
 
• In this case, "**bark**" refers to both the **sound a dog makes** and the **protective outer layer of a tree**.
 
• Because they share the same form (spelling and sound) but distinct definitions, they are classified as homonyms.

Therefore, the correct answer is **homonym**.

 

**Explanation:** *"A dog's **bark** (vocalization) and a tree's **bark** (cortex) are identical in spelling and pronunciation, making them homonyms."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Synonym:** A word or phrase that means exactly or nearly the same as another word (e.g., *"shut"* is a synonym of *"close"*).
 
• **Antonym:** A word opposite in meaning to another (e.g., *"fast"* is an antonym of *"slow"*).
 
• **Hypernym:** A word with a broad meaning that more specific words fall under (e.g., *"flower"* is a hypernym for *"rose"* or *"tulip"*).

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

She insisted (1) / to pay for her meal (2) / despite our objections (3) / to the contrary(4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is located in **part 2** of the sentence due to the incorrect use of the infinitive after the verb "insist."
 
• The verb "**insist**" is typically followed by the preposition "**on**" and a **gerund** (verb+ing) or a "that" clause. It is grammatically incorrect to use a "to-infinitive" directly after it.
 
• To correct the sentence, "**to pay**" should be replaced with "**on paying**."
 
• Alternatively, one could say "insisted that she should pay," but the most concise correction is using the prepositional phrase.

Therefore, the correct answer is **2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"She **insisted on paying** for her meal despite our objections to the contrary."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1) "She insisted"** – This part is correct as the subject and the main verb in the past tense.
 
• **(3) "despite our objections"** – "Despite" is used correctly as a preposition meaning "even though," followed by a noun phrase.
 
• **(4) "to the contrary."** – This is a standard idiomatic expression meaning "to the opposite effect" or "showing the opposite."
 
• **Common Prepositional Errors:** Many verbs in English require specific prepositions (e.g., "agree with," "depend on," "insist on"). Using an infinitive where a preposition + gerund is required is a frequent grammatical mistake.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

He will be arrived (1) / at the airport (2) / before we reach there. (3) / Don't worry(4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in **part 1** of the sentence due to the incorrect formation of the future tense.
 
• The sentence describes an action (arriving) that will be completed before another action (reaching the airport) in the future. This requires the **Future Perfect Tense**.
 
• The structure for Future Perfect is: **Subject + will + have + Past Participle (V3)**.
 
• Therefore, "**will be arrived**" is grammatically incorrect and should be replaced with "**will have arrived**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"He **will have arrived** at the airport before we reach there. Don't worry."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(2) "at the airport"** – This is a correct prepositional phrase indicating a specific location.
 
• **(3) "before we reach there"** – In time clauses referring to the future (using "before," "when," "after"), we use the Simple Present tense ("reach") to refer to the future event. This is grammatically correct.
 
• **(4) "Don't worry."** – This is a standard imperative sentence used to offer reassurance.
 
• **Usage Note:** "Will be arrived" is a common error where the passive voice or a literal translation from other languages is mistakenly applied to the intransitive verb "arrive."

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

Of the two brothers (1) / Ramesh is more tall (2) / than Suresh (3) / by two inches (4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is located in **part 2** of the sentence, specifically in the formation of the comparative adjective.
 
• In English, most one-syllable adjectives (like **tall**, **fast**, **short**) form their comparative degree by adding the suffix "**-er**" rather than using the word "more."
 
• The phrase "**more tall**" is grammatically incorrect and should be replaced with "**taller**."
 
• "More" is generally used for adjectives with three or more syllables (e.g., "more beautiful") or certain two-syllable adjectives.

Therefore, the correct answer is **2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Of the two brothers, Ramesh is **taller** than Suresh by two inches."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1) "Of the two brothers"** – This is a correct way to introduce a comparison between two specific entities. In such cases, the comparative degree is used.
 
• **(3) "than Suresh"** – This part is correct; "than" is the standard conjunction used to introduce the second element in a comparison.
 
• **(4) "by two inches."** – This correctly uses the preposition "by" to indicate the margin or degree of difference between the two subjects.
 
• **Comparison Rule:** When comparing two things, use the **comparative degree** (taller). When comparing three or more, use the **superlative degree** (tallest).

• The adjective "**easy**" is a two-syllable word ending in 'y'. Its superlative form is created by changing the 'y' to 'i' and adding "**-est**" (i.e., **easiest**).
 
• In English grammar, it is incorrect to use "**most**" alongside an adjective that already has the superlative suffix "-est." This creates redundancy.
 
• The phrase "**most easiest**" should be corrected to simply "**easiest**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **2**.

• **Rule for Superlatives:** Use "-est" for one-syllable adjectives and two-syllable adjectives ending in 'y'. Use "most" for adjectives with three or more syllables (e.g., "most difficult"). Never use both together.

• Then, the person adjusts the angle and lighting to ensure the photo is ideal. This is Sentence 1.
 
• Finally, they take the photo successfully with a gentle touch. This is Sentence 3.
